questions.stem: The nurse is giving routine morning care to several clients. In which situation may the nurse proceed on the basis of implied consent?
options: A client extends an arm when the nurse says it is time for a blood pressure check.
A client nods when told the provider will insert a central line later this morning.
A client is asleep when the nurse arrives to give a scheduled subcutaneous injection.
A client pulls the arm away as the nurse approaches with a fingerstick lancet.
optionRationales: Correct. Extending an arm for a routine, low-risk measurement is an action consistent with care, which is implied consent.
Incorrect. A central line is an invasive procedure that requires informed consent obtained by the provider; a nod to the nurse is not enough.
Incorrect. A sleeping client has given no consent by action or word; the nurse wakes the client, explains, and obtains agreement.
Incorrect. Pulling away is a refusal; proceeding would be battery. The nurse stops and explores the reason.
questions.rationale: Implied consent is inferred from the client’s actions, such as extending an arm for vital signs or positioning for an injection, and covers routine, low-risk care. It never replaces informed consent for invasive procedures, which the provider performing the procedure must obtain after explaining the five elements. Silence or sleep is not consent, and pulling away communicates refusal; touching the client anyway would be battery.
questions.takeaway: Cooperative actions = implied consent for routine care; procedures need informed consent, and pulling away is a refusal.
questions.hintContent: Look for a cooperative action that matches a routine, low-risk task.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask: Did the client act in a way that agrees to this specific, low-risk care — or is this a procedure, no response, or a refusal?
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · Consent & Lifespan Laws · pp. 2831

questions.stem: A nurse working in an outpatient clinic reviews the day’s appointments. In most U.S. states, which client may consent to treatment without a parent or guardian?
options: A 16-year-old requesting testing and treatment for chlamydia
A 15-year-old requesting elective cosmetic rhinoplasty
A 14-year-old needing a tonsillectomy who wants parents excluded
A 17-year-old living with parents who needs knee arthroscopy
optionRationales: Correct. All states allow minors to consent to STI testing and treatment, most from age 12.
Incorrect. Elective cosmetic surgery requires parental consent for a minor.
Incorrect. Surgery for a non-emancipated minor requires a parent or guardian’s consent.
Incorrect. A 17-year-old living with parents is not emancipated and needs parental consent for surgery.
questions.rationale: Minors generally need a parent or guardian’s consent unless an exception applies: emergency, emancipation, mature-minor laws, a court order, or a law allowing a specific service. STI care is one of the most widely recognized exceptions; 45 states and DC allow all minors age 12 and older to consent, and the remaining states allow it from age 14 or 16. Elective or surgical procedures for non-emancipated minors require parental consent.
questions.takeaway: Minors may consent to specific services the law allows, such as STI care; surgery usually needs a parent.
questions.hintContent: Which of these services is commonly carved out by law for minors?
questions.hintStrategy: For minor-consent items, check for emancipation, emergency, or a service-specific exception.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · Consent & Lifespan Laws · pp. 2832–2833

questions.stem: A 2-year-old is brought to the emergency department with a spiral fracture of the femur. The parent states the child “fell off the couch,” and later tells a different nurse the child “got caught in the crib.” Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Report the suspected abuse to the designated child protective agency.
Document each caregiver explanation in the caregiver’s own words.
Wait for the radiologist’s report to confirm abuse before making a report.
Confront the parent about the inconsistent explanations.
Ensure the child’s immediate safety and treat the injury and pain.
Tell the parent which staff member is filing the report.
optionRationales: Correct. Nurses are mandated reporters; reasonable suspicion is enough to report.
Correct. Objective documentation of each explanation verbatim supports the investigation.
Incorrect. Proof is not required; delaying the report while awaiting confirmation is inappropriate.
Incorrect. Confronting the caregiver can escalate risk and is the investigators’ role, not the nurse’s.
Correct. Safety and treatment of the injury are immediate priorities.
Incorrect. The reporter’s identity is generally kept confidential from the suspected abuser.
questions.rationale: A spiral fracture in a toddler with changing explanations that do not match the injury are cues for suspected physical abuse. Nurses must report reasonable suspicion in good faith according to policy and directly to the designated agency; proof is not required and investigators carry the burden of proof. The nurse ensures safety, treats the injury, and documents objective findings and statements verbatim. Confronting the caregiver or revealing the reporter can endanger the child. (In North Carolina, any person who suspects child maltreatment must report to the county department of social services.)
questions.takeaway: Report suspicion — not proof — keep the child safe, and document facts verbatim.
questions.hintContent: What does the law require of a nurse who suspects, but cannot prove, abuse?
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options in which the nurse investigates, accuses, or delays the report.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · Consent & Lifespan Laws · pp. 2834

questions.stem: A 16-year-old is seen at a clinic for contraception and is covered by a parent’s health insurance. The adolescent asks, “My mom won’t find out about this, right?” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “Nothing you share with me will ever be told to anyone, so you don’t need to worry.”
“I will need to call your mom before we can start any birth control.”
“Your visit is kept private, but insurance statements sent to your mom may show it.”
“It would be better for you to tell your mom yourself before we go any further.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Absolute confidentiality cannot be promised; there are legal and billing limits.
Incorrect. Many states allow minors to consent to contraceptive services without parental involvement.
Correct. This is honest about confidentiality and its limits, including insurance billing statements.
Incorrect. Encouraging communication can be helpful later, but it does not answer the question honestly and may deter care.
questions.rationale: Adolescents seeking sexual health, contraception, substance use, or mental health care need honest information about confidentiality. Nurses tell them confidentiality will be maintained when possible but cannot be guaranteed — for example, explanation-of-benefits statements sent to a parent who holds the insurance may reveal the service, and safety concerns may require disclosure. Promising total secrecy is dishonest, and requiring parental contact may be inaccurate and drive the adolescent away from care.
questions.takeaway: Promise adolescents confidentiality where possible — never absolute secrecy — and explain the limits, including billing.
questions.hintContent: What could reveal the visit even if the nurse tells no one?
questions.hintStrategy: In confidentiality items, the best answer is honest about limits rather than absolute in either direction.

questions.stem: An off-duty nurse stops to help at the scene of a car crash and begins first aid on an injured driver. Which actions help keep the nurse protected under Good Samaritan laws? Select all that apply.
options: Providing care consistent with the nurse’s training and licensure
Staying with the victim until emergency medical services assumes care
Performing an emergency procedure beyond the nurse’s training to save time
Accepting payment that the victim’s family offers for the help
Giving the arriving paramedics a report of the care provided
Leaving the victim once another bystander says they know first aid
optionRationales: Correct. Protection requires care consistent with the nurse’s training and licensure.
Correct. Once care begins, the nurse must continue until qualified help takes over to avoid abandonment.
Incorrect. Acting beyond training is not consistent with the standard and may not be protected.
Incorrect. Protection generally applies to care given without compensation.
Correct. A handoff report safely transfers care to qualified providers.
Incorrect. Leaving before qualified help assumes care can be abandonment.
questions.rationale: Good Samaritan laws protect healthcare professionals who volunteer emergency aid outside employment, as long as they act within their training, do not accept compensation, avoid gross negligence, and do not abandon the victim. Once care is started, the nurse follows through until someone able to provide appropriate care, such as EMS, takes over, and a handoff report completes that transfer. Another bystander with first aid knowledge is not a qualified transfer.
questions.takeaway: Good Samaritan protection: volunteer, stay within training, and stay until qualified help takes over.
questions.hintContent: Think “free, fit, finish.”
questions.hintStrategy: For each SATA option, check it against each condition of the protection; any violation eliminates it.

questions.stem: A staff nurse discovers that the hospital regularly assigns unlicensed float staff to administer IV medications in the intensive care unit, which violates state law. The nurse wants to be protected as a whistleblower. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Contact a local television station to expose the unsafe practice.
Resign from the position and then report the hospital to the state.
File a complaint with OSHA before talking with anyone at the hospital.
Report the practice in writing through the hospital’s internal chain of command.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Going to the media first bypasses internal channels and the required notice.
Incorrect. Resigning first can forfeit protection; retaliation claims should be filed before resigning.
Incorrect. External agency reporting is appropriate after internal efforts fail or retaliation occurs, not as the first step here.
Correct. Whistleblower protection generally requires a good-faith effort to resolve the issue internally, with written notice and time to correct.
questions.rationale: Whistleblowing is the disclosure of an employer’s unsafe or illegal practices. To qualify for protection, the employee first makes every effort to resolve the problem through internal reporting procedures, involves a violation of a specific law or rule, and gives the employer written notice and reasonable time to correct it, unless the employee has already been threatened or retaliated against. If retaliation occurs, the employee reports to OSHA before resigning.
questions.takeaway: Whistleblowers start with written internal reporting through the chain of command.
questions.hintContent: What step do whistleblower protections expect before going outside the organization?
questions.hintStrategy: Chain-of-command thinking applies: go up internally before going outside, unless retaliation has already occurred.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · Consent & Lifespan Laws · pp. 2833

questions.stem: A nurse administers 50 mcg of fentanyl from a 100-mcg vial and must waste the remaining 50 mcg. The unit is busy. Which action is appropriate?
options: Waste the drug alone and document the amount in the dispensing cabinet.
Ask an unlicensed assistive staff member to observe and cosign the waste.
Save the remaining drug in a locked drawer for the client’s next dose.
Have another licensed nurse observe the waste and cosign the record.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Controlled substance waste must be witnessed; an unwitnessed waste is a diversion risk.
Incorrect. Agency policies require a licensed witness for controlled substance waste.
Incorrect. Single-dose controlled drugs are not saved; keeping the remainder is a diversion and safety risk.
Correct. A licensed nurse who actually observes the waste and cosigns maintains the required accountability.
questions.rationale: The Controlled Substances Act requires strict recordkeeping for controlled drugs from manufacture to administration, and agency policies require that any wasted portion be observed and cosigned by a licensed witness. The witness must actually see the waste, not sign afterward. Unwitnessed waste, saving partial doses, and using unlicensed staff as witnesses all break the chain of accountability and are red flags for diversion.
questions.takeaway: Controlled substance waste requires a licensed witness who actually observes it.
questions.hintContent: Who can legitimately verify the disposal of a controlled substance?
questions.hintStrategy: When options involve controlled drugs, choose the one that preserves accountability and a witnessed record.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · Consent & Lifespan Laws · pp. 2832–2833

questions.stem: A charge nurse is concerned about possible drug diversion on the unit. Which findings involving a staff nurse are cues that warrant reporting? Select all that apply.
options: Frequently wastes opioids without a witness present
Clients report unrelieved pain on her shifts despite documented opioid doses
Often volunteers to give pain medication to other nurses’ clients
Consistently documents pain reassessment 30 minutes after IV opioid doses
Takes frequent unexplained breaks shortly after removing opioids from the cabinet
Asks the pharmacist to clarify an unclear opioid order
optionRationales: Correct. Unwitnessed waste is a common diversion pattern.
Correct. Unrelieved pain despite documented doses suggests the client did not receive the drug.
Correct. Volunteering to medicate others’ clients is a recognized diversion behavior.
Incorrect. Timely pain reassessment is appropriate practice.
Correct. Frequent breaks after removing opioids may indicate diversion or use.
Incorrect. Clarifying an unclear order is safe practice.
questions.rationale: Diversion of controlled substances is a crime, endangers clients, and violates the Controlled Substances Act. Common cues include unwitnessed waste, clients reporting unrelieved pain despite documented doses, volunteering to medicate other nurses’ clients, and frequent unexplained absences after removing opioids. Reassessing pain and clarifying orders are signs of safe practice. The charge nurse reports concerns through the chain of command and per policy rather than investigating alone.
questions.takeaway: Unwitnessed waste, unrelieved client pain, volunteering for others’ opioids, and unexplained breaks are diversion cues.
questions.hintContent: Which behaviors create opportunities to remove drugs without a client receiving them?
questions.hintStrategy: In “recognize cues” SATA items, separate unusual patterns from routine safe practice.

questions.stem: A client with schizophrenia who is not under guardianship is scheduled for elective hernia repair. The client clearly explains the purpose, the risks, and the option of watchful waiting, and then declines the surgery. The client’s adult daughter asks to sign the consent instead. Which action by the nurse is appropriate?
options: Accept the client’s refusal, notify the surgeon, and document the discussion.
Have the daughter sign, because a psychiatric diagnosis makes the client incompetent.
Proceed with surgery under the emergency doctrine to prevent a future emergency.
Ask the psychiatrist to declare the client incompetent before the procedure.
optionRationales: Correct. The client is presumed competent and demonstrates decision-specific capacity, so the refusal stands.
Incorrect. A psychiatric diagnosis does not by itself remove the legal right to decide.
Incorrect. Elective surgery is not an emergency, and the doctrine never overrides a refusal.
Incorrect. Only a court can declare an adult legally incompetent; a clinician assesses capacity.
questions.rationale: Adults are presumed competent unless a court declares otherwise, and capacity is assessed for each specific decision. A client who can explain the purpose, risks, and alternatives and communicate a choice has capacity, regardless of a psychiatric diagnosis. The nurse respects the refusal, notifies the surgeon, and documents. Family members cannot consent for a capable adult, and clinicians assess capacity but cannot declare legal incompetency, which is a court’s role.
questions.takeaway: A diagnosis is not incapacity: an adult who understands and chooses keeps the right to refuse.
questions.hintContent: What did the client demonstrate about understanding this decision?
questions.hintStrategy: When a stem shows the client explaining risks and alternatives, the client has capacity — eliminate surrogate options.

questions.stem: A client being discharged has four new prescriptions and asks, “Which of these will need a brand-new prescription every time, with no refills?” Under the Controlled Substances Act, which medication should the nurse identify?
options: Lorazepam
Acetaminophen with codeine
Oxycodone
Pregabalin
optionRationales: Incorrect. Lorazepam is Schedule IV, with lower abuse potential.
Incorrect. Acetaminophen with codeine is Schedule III.
Correct. Oxycodone is Schedule II: high abuse and dependence potential, accepted medical use, and no refills.
Incorrect. Pregabalin is Schedule V, with the lowest abuse potential.
questions.rationale: The CSA places drugs in Schedules I–V by medical use and abuse potential. Schedule II drugs such as oxycodone, morphine, fentanyl, methadone, and amphetamine have accepted medical use but high abuse and dependence potential, so they require a new prescription for each fill. Acetaminophen with codeine is Schedule III, benzodiazepines such as lorazepam are Schedule IV, and pregabalin is Schedule V. Knowing the schedule helps nurses teach clients about refills, storage, and disposal.
questions.takeaway: Schedule II (e.g., oxycodone, morphine, fentanyl) = highest abuse potential with medical use; no refills.
questions.hintContent: Which drug in the list is an opioid agonist with high abuse potential on its own?
questions.hintStrategy: For schedule items, anchor on one example per schedule and compare.

questions.stem: A woman arrives with an adult client who has a severe traumatic brain injury and states, “I’m his legal guardian. I’ll sign the consent for his feeding tube.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Have the woman sign, because she accompanies the client and knows his history.
Ask the client to sign the consent form to the best of his ability.
Consult the ethics committee about who should make decisions for the client.
Confirm that a copy of the court order of guardianship is in the record.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Presence and familiarity do not establish legal authority to consent.
Incorrect. A severe traumatic brain injury raises doubt about his capacity, and if a court has declared him incompetent his signature is not valid consent; legal authority must be verified first.
Incorrect. An ethics consult is unnecessary if a valid guardianship order exists; verification comes first.
Correct. A guardian must give the healthcare team a copy of the court order validating decision-making authority.
questions.rationale: When a court declares an adult legally incompetent, it appoints a guardian, who must provide a copy of the court order validating authority to make healthcare decisions. The nurse verifies that documentation before accepting the guardian’s consent. Without verification, the nurse cannot know whether the person has legal authority. Ethics consultation may help in disputes but does not replace verifying legal authority.
questions.takeaway: Verify a guardian’s court order before accepting their consent.
questions.hintContent: What document proves a guardian’s authority?
questions.hintStrategy: In “first” items about decision makers, verifying legal authority comes before acting on consent.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · Consent & Lifespan Laws · pp. 2832

questions.stem: A 15-year-old with relapsed acute myelocytic leukemia tells the team he will accept a bone marrow transplant but does not want resuscitation or life support if his heart stops. His parents insist on “everything.” Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Facilitate communication among the adolescent, parents, provider, social worker, and chaplain.
Request an ethics committee consultation according to agency policy.
Tell the adolescent his wishes carry no weight because he is a minor.
Review state law and agency policy on mature-minor decision making.
Enter a do-not-resuscitate order in the record based on the adolescent’s wishes.
Advocate for the adolescent’s voice to be heard in care discussions.
optionRationales: Correct. Open communication among family and team is a key nursing action in this conflict.
Correct. An ethics committee helps resolve conflicts over life-sustaining treatment.
Incorrect. Dismissing the adolescent ignores his developing autonomy and the possibility of mature-minor rights.
Correct. The nurse must know state mature-minor laws and agency policies.
Incorrect. Nurses do not write resuscitation orders; code status is a provider order.
Correct. The nurse advocates for the client’s voice while respecting legal limits.
questions.rationale: When a mature adolescent and parents disagree about life-sustaining treatment, the nurse must know state mature-minor law and agency policy, facilitate open communication among the family, provider, social worker, chaplain, and ethics committee, and advocate for the adolescent’s voice. The nurse does not resolve the conflict alone, dismiss the adolescent, or write code-status orders, which are provider orders. This approach respects both developing autonomy and legal boundaries.
questions.takeaway: In adolescent–parent treatment conflicts, know the law, convene the team and ethics, and advocate for the adolescent’s voice.
questions.hintContent: Which actions are within nursing scope and support shared decision making?
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that are outside nursing scope (writing orders) or that dismiss the client.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · Consent & Lifespan Laws · pp. 2832–2833

questions.stem: During a home visit, a nurse finds an 82-year-old client with dementia lying in soiled bedding with a new stage 3 sacral pressure injury and an empty refrigerator. The adult son who is the live-in caregiver says, “She refuses help, so I leave her alone.” Which action should the nurse take?
options: Report suspected neglect to adult protective services per agency policy.
Ask the son for proof that his mother has refused his help.
Teach the son a turning schedule and reassess at next week’s visit.
Tell the son that he will be arrested if conditions do not improve.
optionRationales: Correct. Signs of neglect in a vulnerable adult require a report to adult protective services.

questions.rationale: Vulnerable or disabled adults who show signs of neglect — untreated pressure injuries, poor hygiene, lack of food — are protected by adult protective services laws, which require reporting when there is reasonable cause to believe protective services are needed. Like child abuse reporting, the nurse reports suspicion and does not investigate or wait for proof. The nurse also addresses the client’s immediate needs, documents objective findings, and notifies the provider. (In North Carolina, this report goes to the county department of social services director, which provides adult protective services.)
questions.takeaway: Suspected neglect of a vulnerable adult is reported to adult protective services without waiting for proof.
